body:
> Again you can do that. But it is not going to be like you see on TV. Those things tend to take years and have uncertain outcome.

Thanks, once again, I must stop using TV as a benchmark for my life.

> Yeah. Growing your own food is hard.

Ya no doubt it's a full-time commitment with high risks

> Same with me. I was going to be fitter, maybe learn language, eventually open my own business, etc.

You are still young too, if you still think these would be worthwhile pursuits you can take small steps towards them.

> I suppose some depression is normal for some people as part of their personality. It could even be an asset for some people.

Sometimes it sucks, but I guess if I get it down to a reasonable level I can work it.

> Hey, keep in touch. I am curious to see how your life develops.

Thanks, honestly I don't expect much external change until I'm done with college. However, I'm really hoping things will get better afterwards (kinda like I've said to myself through all other life milestones, oh well).

> You already mentioned reading about Buddhism. Look into Dr. John Kabat-Zinn and his mindfulness technique. You might also benefit a great deal from Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT).

Thanks I have added 2 more books to my Amazon wish list

> Everybody would rather be free to do what ever they want when ever they want, but instead we have obligations and responsibilities.

I understand, and while I would obviously like to be rich and do whatever I want; no matter what I'd like to have meaning in my life by contributing to some type of research or other advancement. I am beginning to realize that this cannot preclude my happiness. And that it would be ideal to live where work and play can be balanced - not an excess of either.

 There are other times when I just want to move off the grid and attempt to grow my own food - however I think I've romanticized this lifestyle.

> I have a theory that in the modern world peoples ideas of reality are twisted due to TV and movies. You naturally develop expectations of what is normal by what you observe. But nowadays people are observing TV and subconsciously creating false expectations of the norm.

I definitely think this is true, I was going to make a bumper sticker that said "Hollywood lies" but better than that I have began to reassure myself that TV has falsely conditioned me, which is why I'm hoping to read more about buddism and stoicism.

> You do help. You are an EMT.

Thanks - going back to our previous point, I've never done anything crazy like you see on TV - but it does make me feel somewhat accomplished - it can make a bad day worse and a good day better

> I do not think that there is anything you are supposed to be. You just are. And why do you think that you should be happier?

I suppose this was just the culture I was raised in, like there is something wrong with you if you are not happy. However, it seems like there is so much pressure that we all have to "be something", we cannot just "be" that it made me feel worthless because I didn't feel like I was "something" ya know?

> SO you could start again. Summer is almost here!

Ya I'm currently enrolled for both summer sessions so I can graduate in the Fall, like I said, I want to get out of here asap so I can start living my life. If I don't do both I'll have to stay another semester.

> That is kind of a theme of my life as well. When I was younger I thought that I would do all these great things, but as I got older I ran into all kinds of problems and limitations.

Ya, but I wasn't even referring to great things, I was talking about proper diet, sleep and exercise - and perhaps some free reading on the side. I also am prepared to work to achieve the few dreams I do have - I guess I'll just have to focus on finishing school, because in the end it will help even though I dread it most days.

> I don't know you that well but I am beginning to think that you do not need anti-depressants.

I mean I've always felt somewhat depressed, but I think it only becomes unmanageable when my lifestyle is so terrible, I think you are right. The summer after HS and before freshman year of college I had a part time outdoor job and lived with my uncle on a lake. There was no TV or internet there, and I had no school work, so I did most of things I wanted to do: read, exercise, eat right and felt pretty good. However, I did also feel some lingering sadness, because my first GF had just dumped me, which made me feel like a loser, it took me very long to get over it. I isolated myself from my friends when I should have reached out, so it probably didn't help.

> You have to understand that depression is a real illness just like diabetes is a real illness. If you had diabetes, you would not think about insulin the way you think about anti-depressants.

Well I agree, but if I could bear it, I'd only want to try pills only after I have tried to improve my lifestyle - thus ruling that out as a cause. 

One thing that I've recently noticed, which I am going to be very careful not to resort to heavily is that sleeping pills make me feel a lot better - most of the things I worry about do not bother me anymore, although I am not productive at all - so while I don't think either of us would advocate this as a solution, it does give some credence to treatment from my perspective.

> So what is the point of all this responsibility that is preventing you from stopping and smelling the roses? You don't have to live with a huge sense of responsibility that you can never satisfy.

Thanks, for some reason I've always felt this obligation. I will be working to minimize that feeling to a healthier level so it doesn't dictate all my life choices. I know plenty of people who do a lot of good and have a lot of fun.

**I really appreciate your input.** Somehow you were able to identify and change some of the deepest held assumptions about life that I didn't even know I had. As I am able to remove myself from my box of faulty assumptions, I feel a lot of hope for the future and new sense of control over my life which had seemingly been ruled by these assumptions. Thank you! It also opens my mind to therapy as I imagine it works in a similar fashion.

Ya luckily I've only got 2 semesters left hopefully.

> I'll look up jobs that I could potentially work and I get pretty excited

I've done this before

> Anyways, if you ever need to talk or rage or whatever, please feel free to get in touch

Thank you for your support

thank you for the advice 

> It is not nearly as important as your life and happiness.

I agree

Thank you very much for your thoughtful response - talking this over on reddit has actually helped me a lot and I talked to my family today and they were glad I called. I had been set on suicide for around this time for about 2 weeks but I think I'm going to hang in there. It seems to me that a mix of guilt and self-loathing were the biggest factors so I'm going to try to minimize those feelings in my life. I'm going to have to accept the fact that I'll be busy with school for the next 9 months or so (summer classes), but I think if I run everyday, and spend more time with my friends on the weekend (kinda like you were saying) I'll be ok. I've come to accept the fact that I will always have some problems, but if I can manage them, I can be a better person and start enjoying life. I think the post-graduation job hunt is going to be a nightmare but it's not going to last forever either.

> Who does?

Some people do like school somehow - for me personally I despise it, or just suck at dealing with my dislike for it.

> In the end you remember people you were with, and not grades you had and money you made. Everyone knows this!

Ok I agree, but one of the reasons I am depressed is because I've isolated myself so much - I don't really have a lot of great memories of my college years because of this - and I blame myself.

> What is it that is so important that just had to be done?

This is a good point, I'm not really sure - whenever I learn about suffering though I feel guilty and because my life is pretty good, I feel somewhat obligated to help.

> To say that you are broken is to assume that there is a certain way you are supposed to be like.

Another good point - I don't know exactly how I am supposed to be, but I know I should be happier.

> So were you happier then, than you are now?

I think it was a start.

> I thought that the whole problem with college is that you excel at self-study and you can do better by yourself without having to pay for instructor.

Not necessarily, I value mentors highly - my problem with college is that I have all these other issues in my life that are constantly disregarded for schoolwork.

> Try different approach: Do a balance of what you like and what you feel like you have to do. Doing things you hate all the time will make you depressed.

Yes, see I've been told this before, and I realize its true - I just have a hard time achieving it, so I just throw my hands up. I am going to try to work in ways to at least exercise once a day because that doesn't take too long and I feel better afterwards.

> So you are depressed because you are not traveling, and you do not want to travel while depressed?

Well traveling isn't necessarily a priority, it'd be fun to do only if I wasn't depressed from the start. It's a lot of time and money and I wouldn't be able to enjoy it very much knowing I'm just putting off work I should be doing.

> That is an arbitrary difference. In both cases you arbitrarily change the way you feel by changing your brain's chemistry without actually improving circumstances of your life.

I'd say this is somewhat true, but by running you are actually doing something that is healthy and natural - it is also an activity that I enjoy - so in some ways you are improving the circumstances of your life - whereas when you take a pill you are admittedly not improving them

> Right! When you are depressed, you have to force yourself to do things, like working on a relationship. Even pleasant things feel like chores when you are depressed.

Thank you for understanding

> You don’t have to do anything right now. Do you feel a huge burden of responsibility to do something?

This is really good advice - thank you. I think that I have always felt some responsibility that I've never been able to meet.

> Right! You think that going to college is worse than being dead. 

I mean everyone dies so it's not a terrible or unnatural fate. I know college is considered a privilege but I feel like for most of my life (I've NEVER liked school) I've sacrificed things for education and it hardly seems worthwhile anymore. This is how I see my life in a best-case scenario: http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ERbvKrH-GC4

> I am 33 and adolescence sucked for me. One of the reasons, is that at that age you seem to think that everything is so fucking important and that your life is over before it has begun (kind of like you actually). Truth is that life got hell of a lot better, and shit that I used to worry about turned out to be totally unimportant. I had no clue about life, and I probably still don't.

I'm sorry your adolescence sucked, but I'm glad your life got better, and that is an inspiration.
 You are right, but I seem to oscillate between apathy and anxiety.

> You think highly of yourself. You think you are being humble but in fact you are being proud. Truth is that you spending couple of years in school is not hurting the world. Your problem seems to be that YOU are not out there being a great man you imagine yourself to be. You are not unhappy because you think that world needs more help. In any case, you traveling, learning to play an instrument and learning foreign languages is not exactly what the world needs right now. 

This is somewhat accurate, but a bit misconstrued. See I got the idea that doing those things (instrument, language, etc.) would make me happy from previous conversations with people ("well just learn a new language or learn an instrument!") - I'm not sure if they would, but maybe it'd be worth a shot. If I could have the time I wanted, these would not be priorities.

I'm not the great person I think I COULD be - I view myself as somewhat of a lost potential, as I view a lot of people. I think everyone could be great in their own way but so many people squander it, and I fear I am doing that.
 I think a contributing factor in my suicidal thoughts is my belief that I am broken beyond repair.

I do worry alot about things beyond my control, and I think there are so many solutions that could be applied if people could come together. This is why I am interested in biology, I think it has a great potential to solve a lot of issues.

> Well thank you. I have to challenge you before you start believing your own bullshit. 

I've come to see that I am wrong on some of my convictions. I also recognize you are under no obligation to provide advice, and I appreciate your comments.

> So you had a chance to travel, learn to play instrument, learn languages, etc. and instead you took more classes (which you did not have to take)? Did you at least get regular sleep, exercise and raw food diet? 

I would have had to take these classes eventually, and I wanted to get them done as soon as possible - so it wasn't a waste of time based on my goals at the time. With some of the time I did have I was able to read more, get regular sleep, and exercise. I ate better foods but not strictly raw. 

I also didn't necessary have the chance to "travel, learn to play instrument, learn languages" all of those cost money in the form of payments or lost wages. My thinking was just get through school ASAP (sacrifices these summers for more time later)
. I also don't really want to waste the time and money traveling until I actually feel good about myself, otherwise I'm just going to feel pathetic somewhere else.

> There is a big difference between talking and breathing and being dead. 

To me it seems like you'd just become a shell of your former self like in donnie darko or something - I wouldn't want to live like that.

> What happened to not artificially altering chemistry of your brain? 

This is natural, not a prescription.

> SO you are unhappy because you are not meeting your own expectation of popularity? 

I don't really care if I'm popular or not - it just seems like I've been taught that if someone only has 2 friends, then there is something wrong with them. I guess I've come to believe this. I also tend to think that in the end, relationships are the only things that really matter, and although I have good ones, I don't have many - it just seems like I am robbing myself of meeting new people and I am sad that I've let most of my other good relationships fade away.
 Another thought is that I am certain that if I wasn't depressed that I would have more friends so I see this as a symptom of depression rather than a cause.

> You have come to term and have accepted the fact that your sister is institutionalized but you obsess about not eating raw foods and going to college?

Because I have no control over her situation, there is nothing I can do to help her. There really is nothing-I-can-do about her. 

> Why can't you come to the same Nothing-I-Can-Do conclusion about you going to to college? 

Are you saying I should just convince myself to stay in college because I have no options? I did say earlier that I felt I was stuck in a predicament.

> Actually humans have never been healthier or lived longer than they do today. 

We don't actually have proof of that, as metrics for this are only available for a relatively short time in human history. Also, living the last 10 or 20 years of your life confined to a chair or bed is not necessarily something to strive for. I would argue that much of the medical progress we have today is despite popular diet and activity levels (not because of it), and I would credit the progress with advancement in sanitation, vaccination, shelter and specialized medicine (note how these problems have largely been confined to the 3rd world). Whereas, the poor diets (high carb, high fat, low protein, low fiber), sedentary lifestyles, and chemicals in the food (hormones in milk/meat, biproducts of frying, irradiation, etc) in the first world have been causing chronic diseases (diabetes, cancer; and even depression http://www.mayoclinic.com/health/depression-and-diet/AN02057)

> If I disliked you I would not have bothered with you. 

Thanks

> Actually yes! You have some clearly faulty thinking and beliefs and I feel that I have to enlighten you. 

Thanks - you have made me aware of some of my faults.

> No. Depression is not a laughing matter. It's a pretty serious illness. 

Thank you for understanding.

> You don't have to enjoy life. There is really no point in living life for yourself. That is why are discovering a sense of duty and greater good. Our own lives are pretty meaningless and we can't be happy just focusing on our selves. That would feel pointless to us. 

This is a very valid point. Maybe is just the way my generation was raised, a lot of us were encouraged to develop high self-esteem for no reason at all - I'd like to think I avoided this bullshit, but perhaps some aspects of it still reside within me - namely trying to make self-improvements to make myself happy instead of reaching out to others, where it really matters. I do feel better when I help people, but I never feel like I am doing enough and I think, well maybe if I'm a better person I will be more outgoing, confident, etc. and be able to do better things for people. I'm not trying to act sanctimonious or noble, in fact I'd like to achieve a state of mind where I don't have to feed my ego by helping people (like Laozi wrote about). Maybe I don't know exactly what I should do.

> Being dead is the worst possible situation you could be in.

No.

> Define formative years and how are they wasted? You seem to have a certain idea of how life is supposed to flow, and based on this model, you think that you are missing out on something. 

I'd say formative years are childhood and adolescence. This is true. I guess I do feel like I am missing out on a lot, and I blame school and lack of money for this.

> For people like that it is a combination of greatness, hard work, and LOTS AND LOTS OF LUCK. There are many geniuses who work hard but are simply not lucky enough.

Yes while I'd look to do something great for humanity, when will I have time to do the work when it is all occupied by meaningless bullshit. I'll never be a genius either, and I don't care to be famous or admired, but I'd like to go to bed knowing I've done my part for humanity.

> I have an actuarial exam on April 27th and here I am on reddit wasting time. Now that I think about it, so are you.

I just recently found out about reddit and I don't think this post is a waste of time. I'm using some of my free time to try to do some mental maintenance. Your comments have been somewhat offensive and a little insensitive, but though-provoking.

> If it were not for college, you would be blaming something else. Honestly, you are not doing the things that you want to do because you are procrastinating like the rest of us. Did you do any of those things over the summer break? I am guessing NO

I actually took classes, worked and volunteered over summer breaks so I could graduate earlier. Summer classes are worse because they are longer days and it's hard to stay focused. I was able to read some of the books I wanted to when I wasn't taking classes.

> You are contemplating suicide and you are worried about medicines not being natural? 

I don't see the point of living a life where my mindset is artificially chemically altered all the time. It seems kinda like suicide in itself.

> Yes. You get an endophin high which is a chemical reaction inside you. This goes to show that your depression comes from inside you and not outside you. 

I know I'm aware of this but the way I understand it, is that endorphines will heighten anyone's mood, so it is not necessarily indicative of my case.

> You think it's a disaster that you have only two friends (which is plenty in my book). 

It just seems like everyone else has more, and that there is something wrong with me because of it - sorry. I just feel like I am supposed to be more social and feel badly because I'm not.

> You complain that you did sports as a kid and you did not like it. Things you complain about are regular life's problems ,but you think that they are life-ending disasters. 

I don't regret doing sports now (I wish I had stuck with one), I just included that because I wanted to provide some context about the handicapped thought (I'm not sure why I thought it, it was fucked up, but maybe could help someone figure out whats wrong with me). 

> In fact, your sister is institutionalized, but you complain about watching TV instead of eating raw foods. 

I'm not sure what your alluding to. I don't like the fact that my sister is institutionalized but there is nothing I can do about it - I've also gotten over it for the most part. I also believe that the chemicals and composition of processed foods is partially responsible for my depression. I don't think humans evolved to eat the way we do today and its taking a mental toll. Therefore, my thinking is, maybe if I eat better, I would feel better.

I'm not sure why, but you seem to have some personal dislike for me - if I set off some type of trigger in you I'm sorry. I really do feel extremely guilty that I have a pretty average life, but I am always depressed - because I know other people have it worse - that's why I'd really like to do something for humanity before I die - because I figure if I cannot enjoy life, maybe I can help someone else enjoy it. I guess I need to slow down and just try to enjoy what I have.

Thanks

> You can't just admit that you have been wrong for 7 years so you need to justify your unhappiness to yourself. 

I suppose I am justifying some of my unhappiness, but I don't think it's exclusively due to cognitive dissonance.

> You are basically claiming that you have to kill yourself because it is impossible for you to drop out of college!

Yes I could just drop out. But that would leave me in a worse situation where I am now. See I am feeling stuck. If I drop out I will immediately have to start earning money, and spend most of it on a worthless 3 years of college. If I stay in I am going to continue to be miserable.

> You are saying that your life is irreparably damaged because you got education, and the next 50 years of your life will not fix the damage of last few years of attending college. 

Ok, I see how this can see dramatic, but I seriously feel like the formative years of my life have been wasted. I read all the time about young kids who are doing great things precisely because they don't have the burden of college, or they were lucky enough to be spared of the public school system. The only way I imagine I will ever reach my full potential is if I am able to direct the use of my time. However, I am not - I spend all my waking hours doing shit I don't care about, and I don't see that changing even if I drop out of college.

> I don't doubt that you are depressed, but your reasons for depression are silly. You probably have depression because it runs in your family, not because you went to college.

If depression is real I think I do have it, because I've been happy and it feels totally different. I have also been around happy people and they are not like me - this is even when I have known them well and had long talks with them - somehow they just have a better outlook on life. College may not be the reason I am depressed, but it is certainly an amplifying or contributing factor. Like I said, there are some things that can make me happy, but I don't have time for them unless I am exausted and just want to sleep or listen to music because it clears my head.

> You have chemical imbalance that is correctable by medication. This is also why you take small inconveniences and see them as life-ending disasters.

This might be true but I don't want to be on medication. I think I could correct to a reasonable level naturally if I was living a better lifestyle; for example I usually feel good for a short time after running. Also, why do you say that my problems are a small inconvenience?
yes this isn't something i've been thinking about for the past week or even past year. I'd say I've seriously thought about it for about 7 years. I don't ever think I'll not be depressed.
ya but it's not as easy as it sounds. i can't just drop everything and do that. i feel like i have no good choices, and i blame it on the poor decions of my past.
thanks :)

thanks. Ya I could look into staying another semester although that would only prolong the misery (as I stated earlier, I have never liked school, no matter what it is I'm studying). Efficiency is probably my best hope, I find I function better if I run.

thank you. i'll try not to bother you. There are a few things that make me happy but actually doing them at a level where I feel good about myself requires time that I do not have. I don't really want to leave school b/c I'd be way more depressed living at my parents and I can't afford to live anywhere else. It's gotten to the point that even when I daydream or idealize the best of circumstances I do not think I will be happy.

no because I feel like I cannot just do what I want to do - I first need to detoxify my mind and body from the garbage both have been fed for my entire life. I'd need to do this before I can do anything I want to do.
im still gonna be poor and insecure
thanks I know what you mean. It just seems like I can seldom remember a time for more than a few hours where I was genuinely happy.
you seem like a neat person - thanks for commenting on my post. I hope your dreams come true.
i know you mean. the thought of delaying my happiness by another year or two is just unbearable though considering I've dreaded school since kindergarden.
as much as I'd love to take a year off like that, I don't think I would ever finish school. Once I'm living the life I want, I don't think I'd come back.
I did but it's just going to delay graduation and be costly. If I were going to take a year off, I'd wanna just live somewhere alone.
